findings.title: Division by zero on empty order
findings.explanation: AveragePricePerItem divides the subtotal by items.Count without checking for an empty list. For an empty input, decimal division by zero throws DivideByZeroException at runtime.
findings.reason: Identifies DivideByZeroException from dividing by items.Count on an empty order, the core of label #2.

findings.title: Threshold comparison contradicts comment
findings.explanation: The comment on line 24 says orders of 500 or more get an extra 5 percent, but the code uses 'subtotal > 500m', so an order of exactly 500 does not qualify. Either the comment or the operator is wrong, and the mismatch can cause a billing dispute.
findings.reason: Strict > 500 contradicts the 'or more' comment, so an order of exactly 500 misses the extra discount.

findings.title: No validation of order line values
findings.explanation: Subtotal accepts any quantity and unit price, including negative or zero values. Negative quantities or prices would silently reduce totals and could produce negative or incorrect charges. Null lines or a null collection would throw an unhelpful NullReferenceException.
findings.reason: Speculative input-validation advice; nothing in this code requires it and it is not a concrete defect.

findings.title: Magic numbers in discount rates
findings.explanation: The discount percentages 0.10m, 0.05m, and the extra 0.05m on line 27 are embedded directly in the logic. Changing pricing policy requires editing code, and the repeated 0.05m value is easy to update inconsistently.
findings.reason: Magic-number remark is a style preference; the constants are readable in a small switch.

findings.title: Free shipping evaluated on discounted total without clear intent
findings.explanation: Free shipping is decided using the discounted amount, so a discount can push an order below the threshold and add a fee. This behavior is probably intended but is not documented, and a reviewer could easily assume the pre-discount subtotal was used.
findings.reason: Shipping on the discounted total is plausible intended behavior; the finding itself admits that and only asks for documentation.

findings.title: Unnecessary materialization in Total
findings.explanation: The lines enumerable is materialized with ToList() and then passed to Subtotal, which enumerates it again. This is a minor cost, but it also means the method enumerates the input more than once when it is a deferred query.
findings.reason: Materializing with ToList() prevents multiple enumeration, and Subtotal then enumerates the list once. The claim is wrong.

findings.title: SQL injection via unvalidated sortBy in ORDER BY
findings.explanation: The caller-supplied sortBy string is interpolated directly into the SQL text, so any input such as "IssuedOn; DROP TABLE dbo.Invoices" or a subquery is executed by the database. Parameters cannot be used for column names, so the value must be validated against an allowlist before it is put into the query.
findings.reason: Describes SQL injection through unvalidated sortBy interpolated into ORDER BY, same as label 1.

findings.title: Allowlist defined but never enforced
findings.explanation: SortColumns is declared as a case-insensitive allowlist of valid sort columns, but SearchAsync never checks sortBy against it. The protection the field was clearly meant to provide is absent, so the injection risk above is fully exposed.
findings.reason: Describes cs-02-invoice-repository#1 but at lines 10-13, outside the window. Allowlist defined but not applied to sortBy is the root cause of the label's injection defect; label explicitly mentions the allow-list no longer applied.

findings.title: SqlConnection is never disposed
findings.explanation: DeleteOlderThanAsync creates a SqlConnection without a using or await using declaration. The command is disposed, but the connection is not, so the connection is not returned to the pool promptly and can leak under load or if an exception is thrown.
findings.reason: SqlConnection in DeleteOlderThanAsync is not disposed, leaking pooled connections.

findings.title: LIKE wildcards in user input are not escaped
findings.explanation: The customer value is wrapped in % characters and used in a LIKE pattern without escaping. Any % or _ typed by the user acts as a wildcard, so searches can match more rows than intended.
findings.reason: Unescaped wildcards in a user-supplied search are normally intended behavior for a contains search; not a real defect, and no injection risk since it's parameterized.

findings.title: Missing ConfigureAwait(false) in library code
findings.explanation: This repository is library code, but the awaits on OpenAsync, ExecuteReaderAsync, ReadAsync, and ExecuteNonQueryAsync do not use ConfigureAwait(false). This can force continuations back onto a captured synchronization context, which can cause deadlocks in some hosts and adds unnecessary overhead.
findings.reason: ConfigureAwait(false) advice is a best-practice preference; not a meaningful defect here (ASP.NET Core has no sync context) and mislabeled as performance.

findings.title: Password reset token generated with non-cryptographic Random
findings.explanation: System.Random is a predictable PRNG, and a new instance per call can produce repeated or guessable sequences. Reset tokens must come from a CSPRNG. The range 100000 to 999999 also gives only about 900,000 possible values, and Random.Next's exclusive upper bound means 999999 is never issued.
findings.reason: Identifies non-cryptographic System.Random and small six-digit space for reset tokens, same as label.

findings.title: Short token with no attempt limiting or expiry-independent brute-force protection
findings.explanation: A 6-digit token gives roughly one million possibilities. RedeemAsync accepts unlimited guesses for a user within the 30-minute lifetime, with no attempt counter, lockout, or rate limit, so an attacker can brute-force the token.
findings.reason: Missing attempt limiting/rate limiting on redemption is a genuine weakness given a six-digit token, and it is not covered by the labels, which concern the token's generation. It is a distinct defect in RedeemAsync.

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted
findings.explanation: The condition returns false when saved.ExpiresAt > now, which means the token is still valid. Valid tokens are therefore rejected, and expired tokens (ExpiresAt <= now) fall through and can be redeemed.
findings.reason: Describes the inverted expiry comparison on line 29 exactly.

findings.title: Check-then-delete is not atomic, allowing a token to be redeemed more than once
findings.explanation: The token is validated, then deleted in a separate step. Two concurrent RedeemAsync calls with the correct token can both pass validation before either deletes it, so the same reset can be used twice.
findings.reason: Non-atomic check-then-delete permits concurrent double redemption of a reset token; a genuine race not covered by the labels.

findings.title: Unsalted fast hash of low-entropy token
findings.explanation: The token is stored as an unsalted SHA-256 hash. Because the token space is only about one million values, anyone who obtains the stored hashes can recover every token by brute force in a short time.
findings.reason: Hash-only storage of a short token is a mild concern, but it is mainly a consequence of the low entropy already labeled. Salting would not fix it, and the finding is speculative.

findings.title: Missing ConfigureAwait(false) on awaited store calls
findings.explanation: This is library-style service code, and the awaited store calls in IssueAsync and RedeemAsync capture the caller's synchronization context unnecessarily.
findings.reason: ConfigureAwait advice is a style/best-practice remark that does not matter in this code; it is not a defect.

findings.title: Path traversal via client-supplied file name on upload
findings.explanation: storedName is taken directly from file.FileName, which is client-controlled. A name containing directory segments such as "../" or an absolute path can make Path.Combine resolve outside the uploads folder, allowing arbitrary file writes on the server. Path.Combine also discards the folder when the second argument is rooted.
findings.reason: Client-supplied file name used as stored name allows traversal out of the uploads folder, which is the core of label #1.

findings.title: Path traversal in Download via route parameter
findings.explanation: The id route value is combined with the uploads folder without validation. A request such as /api/documents/..%2F..%2Fappsettings.json can read files outside the uploads directory. File.Exists confirms the target before it is served.
findings.reason: Download combines the id with the path unvalidated, enabling path traversal; same as label #3.

findings.title: No authentication or authorization on upload and download endpoints
findings.explanation: Neither Upload nor Download declares any authorization requirement. Any anonymous caller can write files to the server and read any stored document, which is a serious exposure for a documents API.
findings.reason: The file shows no auth configuration. Authorization may be applied globally or via middleware, so this is speculative.

findings.title: File type validated only by extension
findings.explanation: The extension comes from the client-supplied file name and the content is never inspected. A file such as malware.exe renamed to .pdf, or any content labelled .png, passes validation and is stored and later served.
findings.reason: Validation by extension only is a genuine weakness; content is never checked and the file is later served from the same API.

findings.title: Synchronous CopyTo inside an async method and unnecessary buffering
findings.explanation: file.CopyTo blocks a thread inside an async action and ignores the cancellation token. The code also copies the upload into a MemoryStream and then calls ToArray, which duplicates the full 10 MB payload in memory per request.
findings.reason: Synchronous CopyTo and in-memory buffering with ToArray are exactly the performance problem in label #2.

findings.title: Existing files are silently overwritten
findings.explanation: Using the original file name means a second upload with the same name replaces the earlier document. The API then returns the same id for two different documents, which causes data loss.
findings.reason: Same-name uploads overwriting each other is explicitly part of label #1.

findings.title: No null check on the uploaded file
findings.explanation: If the request does not include the file part, file is null and file.Length throws a NullReferenceException, which surfaces as a 500 error instead of a 400 response.
findings.reason: With [ApiController], a missing IFormFile parameter triggers automatic model validation returning 400, so null does not reach the action.

findings.title: Client-controlled file name written to logs
findings.explanation: storedName originates from the client and is logged unsanitized, which allows log forging through newline or control characters.
findings.reason: Log forging is minor here; structured logging with a placeholder does not allow injecting new log entries in typical providers.

findings.title: Hardcoded size limit duplicated in the message
findings.explanation: The text "10 MB" is hardcoded separately from MaxBytes, so changing the constant leaves the message incorrect.
findings.reason: A hardcoded message duplicating the constant is a trivial style remark, not a defect.

findings.title: Blocking on async call with .Result
findings.explanation: GetRateAsync(...).Result blocks the calling thread while waiting for an async HTTP call. In contexts with a SynchronizationContext (ASP.NET classic, WPF, WinForms) this can deadlock, and in server code it wastes thread pool threads under load.
findings.reason: Describes blocking on .Result at line 20, with deadlock and thread-pool starvation risk.

findings.title: Async method contains no await
findings.explanation: ConvertAsync is declared async and returns Task<decimal> but contains no await, which generates a compiler warning and misleads readers about its behavior. The actual asynchronous work is hidden behind a blocking .Result call.
findings.reason: The async method does lack an await, but this is a minor symptom of the .Result problem. Fixing .Result fixes it. It is not a separate defect and is partly covered by label #2.

findings.title: Non-thread-safe static dictionary
findings.explanation: _rates is a plain Dictionary<string, ExchangeRate> accessed from concurrent requests. Concurrent reads and writes can corrupt the dictionary, cause exceptions, or return inconsistent data. The file already imports System.Collections.Concurrent but does not use it.
findings.reason: Static non-thread-safe Dictionary accessed concurrently.

findings.title: Check-then-act race condition on cache and multiple fetches
findings.explanation: The cache is read, found stale or missing, fetched over HTTP, then written without synchronization. Concurrent callers for the same key will all perform the HTTP request (thundering herd), and the cache read and write are not atomic.
findings.reason: The race on the dictionary is the labeled issue. The thundering-herd duplicate fetch is a benign inefficiency, and the atomicity concern is the same root problem as label #1.

findings.title: Static cache shared across instances ignores injected dependencies
findings.explanation: Because _rates is static, all ExchangeRateCache instances share entries regardless of which HttpClient or TimeProvider they were constructed with. This makes testing hard and can leak rates between tests or tenants.
findings.reason: A static cache in an instance class with injected HttpClient and TimeProvider leaks state between instances and tests, which is a genuine design flaw.

findings.title: No ConfigureAwait on awaited call in library code
findings.explanation: This is library code that may be called from contexts with a SynchronizationContext. The awaited HTTP call does not use ConfigureAwait(false), which can cause unnecessary context switching and contributes to deadlock risk when combined with blocking calls.
findings.reason: ConfigureAwait advice is a best practice, not a real defect in this code, and it does not apply to ASP.NET Core.

findings.title: Rate value not validated
findings.explanation: The response rate is accepted without validation. A zero, negative, or otherwise invalid rate from the remote service would be cached for 10 minutes and used for all conversions, silently producing wrong payment amounts.
findings.reason: A zero or negative rate from the remote service would be cached and used for payment conversions without any validation, which is a real correctness risk.

findings.title: Missing input validation on currency codes and amount
findings.explanation: from and to are not checked for null, empty, or malformed values before being used in the cache key and URL. Currency codes are also compared case-sensitively, so 'usd' and 'USD' would be treated as different pairs.
findings.reason: This is speculative validation advice. Case sensitivity is minor and unsupported by the code context.

findings.title: Hardcoded rounding precision
findings.explanation: The magic number 2 assumes all currencies have two decimal places. Currencies such as JPY use zero, and others like KWD use three, so this can produce incorrect payment amounts.
findings.reason: Rounding to 2 decimals is wrong for currencies like JPY or KWD, so payment amounts would be incorrect.

findings.title: Retry loop performs only two attempts (off-by-one)
findings.explanation: The loop condition `attempt < MaxAttempts` with MaxAttempts = 3 runs only attempts 1 and 2. The constant name and the check on line 19 both imply three attempts, so one retry is silently lost. The `attempt < MaxAttempts` guards on lines 19 and 28 are also inconsistent with the intended count.
findings.reason: Identifies the off-by-one in the loop condition at line 13 that allows only two attempts.

findings.title: New HttpClient created per call causes socket exhaustion
findings.explanation: Creating and disposing an HttpClient for each call bypasses IHttpClientFactory and its handler pooling. Under load this exhausts sockets and causes TIME_WAIT buildup and DNS staleness. The GetTrackingStatusAsync method uses the factory, so the two methods are inconsistent.
findings.reason: Describes per-call HttpClient creation bypassing the factory and causing socket exhaustion.

findings.title: Hardcoded API base address
findings.explanation: The shipper endpoint URL is hardcoded in the method. It cannot be changed per environment (test, staging, production) without a code change, and it differs from the factory-configured 'shipping' client used elsewhere.
findings.reason: The hardcoded base URL is a configuration remark on the same line as the HttpClient defect, and it is speculative as a separate issue. The core problem is already captured by the HttpClient label.

findings.title: CreateShipment has no retry or transient-failure handling
findings.explanation: CreateShipmentAsync throws on any non-success status and does not retry 429 or 5xx responses, unlike GetTrackingStatusAsync. This is inconsistent behavior, and transient failures will surface as failed shipment creation.
findings.reason: Not retrying a POST that creates a shipment is arguably correct, since it is non-idempotent and a retry could create duplicates. Adding retry would be questionable advice.

findings.title: Unreachable throw indicates control-flow problem
findings.explanation: The final throw is documented as 'Unreachable', but the loop can complete without returning when the retry branch is taken on the last iteration. The throw is not truly unreachable and its message is misleading.
findings.reason: Describes cs-06-shipping-client#1 but at lines 35-35, outside the window. The 'Unreachable' throw being reachable is the consequence described in label 1, caused by the off-by-one loop bound.

findings.title: Magic number in backoff calculation
findings.explanation: The base delay of 200 ms and the multiplier 2 are embedded in the expression without a name, which makes tuning and understanding the policy harder.
findings.reason: Magic numbers in a small backoff helper are a style preference with no real defect.

findings.title: Missing ConfigureAwait(false) on awaits in library code
findings.explanation: The awaits in this library class do not use ConfigureAwait(false), so continuations may be marshaled back to a synchronization context. This can cause deadlocks or unnecessary overhead if callers block or use a UI/ASP.NET classic context.
findings.reason: ConfigureAwait(false) is not needed in modern ASP.NET Core code and this is a best-practice remark that does not matter here.

findings.title: Date range excludes the last day despite documentation
findings.explanation: The summary says both the first and last day are included, but 'end' is set to the midnight at the start of the 'to' date and the filter uses 'PlacedAt < end'. Orders placed on the 'to' date are silently dropped from the report.
findings.reason: Same defect: end is midnight at the start of the 'to' date with a < filter, so the last day is excluded.

findings.title: N+1 query: one database round trip per customer
findings.explanation: Inside the loop, a separate SingleAsync query is executed for every customer group. For N customers this issues N extra queries, which is slow and scales poorly.
findings.reason: Describes the per-customer SingleAsync query in the loop, which is the N+1 problem.

findings.title: All orders in the range are loaded into memory for client-side aggregation
findings.explanation: The method pulls every order in the date range into a list and then groups and sums in memory. For large date ranges this uses significant memory and transfers far more data than needed.
findings.reason: Describes cs-07-sales-report#2 but at lines 17-19, outside the window. The label's description covers loading every order into memory and grouping in the database instead; this finding describes that same inefficiency in the same code.

findings.title: SingleAsync throws if the customer does not exist
findings.explanation: If an order references a CustomerId that has no matching customer record, SingleAsync throws an exception and the whole report fails. There is also no handling for this condition.
findings.reason: Orders presumably have a customer foreign key, so a missing customer is unlikely; this is speculative and not a defect in this code.

findings.title: Average throws on an empty result
findings.explanation: Enumerable.Average on an empty decimal sequence throws InvalidOperationException. A customer with no orders causes an unhandled exception instead of a sensible result.
findings.reason: Enumerable.Average throws InvalidOperationException on an empty sequence for a customer with no orders.

findings.title: Aggregation performed on the client instead of the database
findings.explanation: AverageOrderValueAsync materializes every order total for the customer just to compute an average. This is unnecessary data transfer when the database can compute the average.
findings.reason: Fetching all totals to compute an average client-side is wasteful. The database can compute AverageAsync, which also can address the empty case. This is a genuine but minor performance issue not covered by the labels.

findings.title: Hardcoded fallback JWT signing key
findings.explanation: If the Jwt:SigningKey configuration value is missing, the code silently falls back to a hardcoded string that is visible in source control. Anyone who knows this default can forge tokens that pass signature validation, and the fallback can reach production unnoticed because nothing fails at startup.
findings.reason: Describes the hardcoded fallback signing key on line 11, which is the same defect as the label.

findings.title: Token lifetime validation disabled
findings.explanation: ValidateLifetime = false means expired JWTs are accepted indefinitely. A leaked or stolen token stays valid forever, which defeats expiration-based session control.
findings.reason: ValidateLifetime = false lets expired tokens through, which is the labeled defect.

findings.title: Full bearer token written to logs
findings.explanation: The log entry includes the complete Authorization header, which contains the bearer credential. Anyone with access to the logs can replay the token, and logs are often retained and shared more widely than secrets should be.
findings.reason: The Authorization header containing the bearer token is written to the logs, matching the label.

findings.title: Issuer and audience may be null while validation is enabled
findings.explanation: ValidateIssuer and ValidateAudience are true, but ValidIssuer and ValidAudience come from configuration with no null check. If either key is absent, validation fails for every token, or the setup behaves unpredictably. Misconfiguration is not reported at startup.
findings.reason: If issuer or audience is missing, validation fails closed and rejects every token. That is a misconfiguration that shows up immediately, not a security defect, and the claim of unpredictable behavior is speculative.

findings.title: Normalize can throw on malformed Unicode input
findings.explanation: string.Normalize throws ArgumentException when the input contains unpaired surrogates or other invalid UTF-16. ToSlug only guards against null, so untrusted titles with invalid characters will propagate an unhandled exception.
findings.reason: In .NET Core/5+, string.Normalize does throw ArgumentException on invalid UTF-16 such as unpaired surrogates. An unguarded call on untrusted titles is a genuine robustness issue, even though the contract only mentions null.

findings.title: Truncation can split words mid-token
findings.explanation: The loop stops at exactly MaxLength characters, so long titles are cut in the middle of a word, which produces unreadable slugs such as 'the-quick-brown-fo'.
findings.reason: Truncating at MaxLength is the documented behavior ('at most MaxLength characters'). Mid-word cuts are a stylistic preference, not a defect.

findings.title: Empty slug returned for titles without ASCII alphanumerics
findings.explanation: Titles made only of non-Latin letters or punctuation produce an empty string, which can yield empty or colliding URLs with no signal to the caller.
findings.reason: Titles with no ASCII alphanumerics (e.g. all CJK or punctuation) return an empty slug, which can produce empty or colliding URLs. A careful reviewer would want that handled or documented.

findings.title: Null Name or Email causes exception on read
findings.explanation: The Customer record declares Name and Email as non-nullable strings, but reader.GetString(1) and reader.GetString(2) throw InvalidCastException when the column contains NULL. Any row with a NULL Name or Email makes FindAsync fail.
findings.reason: The schema is unknown; nothing indicates Name or Email columns are nullable, and the record declares them non-nullable. GetString on NULL throws SqlNull exception, but this is speculative and the code is consistent with its model.

findings.title: No length validation against NVARCHAR(200)
findings.explanation: The parameter is declared with size 200, but the name is not checked for length before it is sent. A longer name causes a database error at execution time instead of a clear argument validation error.
findings.reason: With SqlParameter size 200, longer strings are silently truncated by the client (not a DB error), and anyway missing length validation is a speculative best-practice remark rather than a real defect.

findings.title: Missing ConfigureAwait(false) on awaits in library code
findings.explanation: This class lives in a data layer library and every await captures the synchronization context. This can cause deadlocks in callers that block on the result and adds unnecessary context switching.
findings.reason: ConfigureAwait(false) is a style/best-practice preference; modern .NET has no sync context by default, and the deadlock only arises from callers blocking on async code.

findings.title: Subject claim lookup may fail under default JWT claim mapping
findings.explanation: User.FindFirst("sub") relies on the raw JWT claim type. By default, ASP.NET Core's JwtBearer handler maps inbound claims (MapInboundClaims = true), so "sub" is rewritten to ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier and FindFirst("sub") returns null. Every authenticated request would then throw InvalidOperationException.
findings.reason: This depends on unseen auth configuration. The code may use MapInboundClaims = false, and the finding itself says only that it "may fail". It is speculative and does not show a defect in this file.

findings.title: Missing subject claim produces a 500 instead of an authentication failure
findings.explanation: When the signed-in user lacks a subject claim, the controller throws InvalidOperationException, which surfaces as an HTTP 500. This is an authentication/authorization problem and should be reported as 401 or 403.
findings.reason: An authorized user without a subject claim is a server or configuration invariant violation. Throwing here is a deliberate choice, and [Authorize] already handles unauthenticated callers. This is a preference remark, not a defect.

findings.title: Required and StringLength do not reject whitespace-only SKUs
findings.explanation: [Required] only rejects null or empty strings. A whitespace-only SKU such as "   " passes validation and is forwarded to the service.
findings.reason: Whether [Required] rejects whitespace is wrong as stated: AllowEmptyStrings is false by default, and the attribute rejects whitespace-only strings. The finding's premise is incorrect.

findings.title: Hardcoded database credentials
findings.explanation: The connection string contains a production server name, username 'admin' and password 'admin123' as compile-time constants. Anyone with access to the source or compiled assembly can read them, and they cannot be rotated without a redeploy.
findings.reason: Hardcoded DB credentials in connection string constant.

findings.title: Hardcoded API key
findings.explanation: The API key is embedded as a constant and is also returned to callers of AuthenticateUserAsync (line 109), exposing it to every authenticated user.
findings.reason: Hardcoded API key constant on line 11.

findings.title: Hardcoded encryption key
findings.explanation: The encryption key is a source-code constant, so anyone who can read the code can decrypt data protected with it.
findings.reason: The hardcoded EncryptionKey constant on line 12 is a genuine defect, and it is not covered by label 6, which addresses the key/IV on lines 44-45. It is also unused, but remains a secret in source.

findings.title: Shared mutable connection field
findings.explanation: A single SqlConnection is held for the lifetime of the service and reused across concurrent calls. SqlConnection is not thread-safe, and the field is not readonly.
findings.reason: A single SqlConnection shared across concurrent calls is not thread-safe, which is a genuine design issue distinct from the leak label.

findings.title: Connection opened in constructor and never disposed
findings.explanation: The constructor opens a database connection synchronously. The class does not implement IDisposable, so the connection is never closed or disposed. This leaks connections and blocks the caller during construction.
findings.reason: Connection opened in constructor and never disposed.

findings.title: SQL injection via table name and user ID
findings.explanation: tableName is interpolated directly into the SQL text, and userId is concatenated into the WHERE clause. Attackers can inject arbitrary SQL or read any table.
findings.reason: SQL injection via tableName and userId interpolation.

findings.title: Sensitive data logged to console
findings.explanation: Each retrieved row writes a log line tied to the user ID, and the data is then returned. Logging per-user sensitive-data access leaks identifiers into logs and adds I/O to the read loop.
findings.reason: The log line only contains the user ID, not the sensitive data itself, so the claim of sensitive data leaking is overstated and the issue is minor.

findings.title: Weak DES encryption with static key and IV
findings.explanation: DESCryptoServiceProvider is obsolete and DES is cryptographically broken. The key and IV are fixed, the IV is identical to the key, and both are derived from a short ASCII literal. Identical plaintexts always produce identical ciphertexts.
findings.reason: Mainly describes obsolete DES; also mentions the static key/IV. The primary focus is DES weakness.

findings.title: Path traversal in user file read
findings.explanation: fileName is concatenated into a path under C:\UserFiles without validation. Values such as '..\..\Windows\win.ini' allow reading arbitrary files on the server.
findings.reason: Path traversal through fileName.

findings.title: Command injection via cmd.exe
findings.explanation: The user-supplied command is passed unvalidated to cmd.exe /c. Any shell metacharacter such as & or | lets an attacker execute arbitrary commands on the server.
findings.reason: Command injection via cmd.exe /c.

findings.title: Process object not disposed
findings.explanation: The Process instance is created but never disposed, which leaks native handles. WaitForExit is also called after reading output, and no timeout is applied, so a hung process blocks the caller indefinitely.
findings.reason: Process is not disposed, and there is no timeout. This is a genuine resource-handling issue not covered by any label.

findings.title: Cross-site scripting via unencoded comment
findings.explanation: The raw comment text is embedded in HTML without encoding. Any markup or script in the comment will be rendered by the browser.
findings.reason: XSS from unencoded comment in HTML.

findings.title: Log injection and synchronous file write in request handler
findings.explanation: User input is written to the log without sanitizing line breaks, so attackers can forge log entries. The log entry also has no trailing newline, so consecutive entries run together. File.AppendAllText blocks the request thread.
findings.reason: Log injection from unsanitized user input written to the log file, plus missing newline, is a genuine defect not covered by labels.

findings.title: Plaintext password comparison in SQL
findings.explanation: The password is compared directly in the SQL query, which implies it is stored in plaintext in the Users table. A database breach then exposes every user's password.
findings.reason: Plaintext password comparison in the query.

findings.title: Connection string with credentials in exception message
findings.explanation: The exception text includes the full connection string, which contains the database password. Anything that logs or displays this exception discloses the credentials. The message also reveals whether the username exists to the caller.
findings.reason: Connection string put in the exception message.

findings.title: API key returned to caller
findings.explanation: The authentication response includes the service API key, so any caller who logs in receives a secret credential.
findings.reason: API key returned to caller.

findings.title: Exception re-thrown as generic Exception with lost context
findings.explanation: The SqlException is wrapped in a generic Exception, which discards the exception type and original stack trace. The message also embeds the connection string.
findings.reason: Wrapped exception exposes connection string and loses the original exception.

findings.title: Authentication failure modeled as exception
findings.explanation: Invalid credentials are an expected outcome, not an exceptional condition. Using UnauthorizedAccessException for flow control makes the method harder to use and is costly under brute-force attempts.
findings.reason: This is a design/style preference about using exceptions for control flow, not a real defect that needs fixing.

findings.title: Static counter is not thread-safe
findings.explanation: _counter is a static field incremented with ++ and read without synchronization. Concurrent calls can produce duplicate or skipped IDs.
findings.reason: Describes seed-01-user-data-service#14 but at lines 117-117, outside the window. Non-atomic increment of shared static counter.

findings.title: Blocking sleep in ID generation
findings.explanation: Thread.Sleep(1) blocks the calling thread on every ID request for no evident reason. This severely limits throughput under load.
findings.reason: Thread.Sleep(1) in ID generation needlessly blocks threads and hurts throughput; a genuine defect not covered by labels.

findings.title: Loop creates unmanaged resources on every iteration
findings.explanation: The loop runs one million times and creates a FileStream that is never disposed and writes a file per iteration, which fails or exhausts file handles. It also creates a new HttpClient each iteration, causing socket exhaustion. The MemoryStream is unused and not disposed.
findings.reason: Undisposed FileStream, MemoryStream and HttpClient in a loop.

findings.title: Magic number in loop bound
findings.explanation: The literal 1000000 is hardcoded with no named constant or explanation of its meaning.
findings.reason: A magic-number remark is a style comment with no real impact here.

findings.title: Predictable security token from fixed-seed Random
findings.explanation: System.Random seeded with the constant 123 produces a fully deterministic sequence. Anyone who knows the seed can predict every generated token.
findings.reason: Fixed-seed Random used for security tokens.

findings.title: Awaits missing ConfigureAwait(false) and no cancellation support
findings.explanation: The async data-access method awaits without ConfigureAwait(false) and accepts no CancellationToken. In library code this can cause unnecessary context capture and prevents callers from cancelling long queries.
findings.reason: ConfigureAwait and CancellationToken advice is speculative best-practice and not a defect here.

findings.title: Obsolete System.Data.SqlClient namespace
findings.explanation: System.Data.SqlClient is deprecated in favor of Microsoft.Data.SqlClient, which receives the ongoing security and feature updates.
findings.reason: The deprecated namespace is a preference or maintenance remark, not a defect in this code.

findings.title: Interval never cleared (memory leak)
findings.explanation: The setInterval created in the effect is never cleared, and the effect returns no cleanup function. The timer keeps running after unmount and logs every second, leaking resources.
findings.reason: Interval never cleared, no cleanup returned.

findings.title: XSS via dangerouslySetInnerHTML
findings.explanation: renderUserComment injects raw user-controlled text as HTML. Any user name containing script or event-handler markup will execute in the dashboard origin. It is called with user.name at line 152.
findings.reason: XSS via dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

findings.title: Hardcoded API key and admin password in client code
findings.explanation: An API key and an admin password are embedded in the frontend bundle and sent with every request. Anyone can read them from the shipped JavaScript or network traffic.
findings.reason: Mainly describes hardcoded API key (and admin password); it spans lines 32-37 and touches both labels, but leads with the API key.

findings.title: Credentials sent over unencrypted HTTP
findings.explanation: The request uses http:// so the Authorization header and admin password are transmitted in plaintext and can be intercepted or altered.
findings.reason: Credentials over plain HTTP.

findings.title: Passwords and API key persisted to localStorage
findings.explanation: User passwords are written to localStorage in plaintext, and the API key is stored there too. Any XSS or browser extension can read them, and they persist across sessions.
findings.reason: Mainly about passwords stored in localStorage (also mentions API key).

findings.title: No validation of API response shape
findings.explanation: userData.users is assumed to exist and be an array. If the response lacks it, setUsers receives undefined and the subsequent .map throws, with no meaningful error to the user.
findings.reason: userData.users is used without validation; a missing field causes setUsers(undefined) and a crash on users.map. Genuine robustness defect.

findings.title: Errors reported via alert with no UI error state
findings.explanation: Failures are surfaced with alert() and the error is stringified. There is no persistent error state, retry option, or accessible message, so the UI cannot show loading or error states properly.
findings.reason: alert for errors is a UX/style preference, not a defect.

findings.title: SQL built from unsanitized input (dead code, logged)
findings.explanation: The search term is interpolated into a SQL string, which is then logged. Even though the query is never executed, this pattern invites SQL injection if it is ever wired to a backend, and logging it leaks search input.
findings.reason: SQL string built from raw input and logged to the console. It is dead code, but a careful reviewer would still flag the injection pattern and the logging of search input.

findings.title: Search overwrites the source user list
findings.explanation: searchUsers filters and replaces the users state. Clearing the search or typing a different term cannot restore the original list, because the filtered-out users are gone. It also filters only the local state, not the server data.
findings.reason: Search overwrites the users list so it cannot be restored.

findings.title: Infinite loop freezes the UI
findings.explanation: If a user has an empty or missing name, the condition fails and processed never increments, so the while loop never terminates and blocks the main thread. The function is also unused.
findings.reason: Infinite loop when user has no name.

findings.title: Concurrent updates map responses to wrong users and ignore errors
findings.explanation: Responses are mapped to users by array index rather than by userId, so unrelated users get overwritten with 'Updated-N' names. The fetch responses are never checked for ok status, and the returned promise is neither awaited nor caught, so failures are silent and unhandled.
findings.reason: Index used instead of userId; errors ignored.

findings.title: Allocates one million large objects in the render path
findings.explanation: handleLargeDataOperation creates a million objects, each with a roughly 1000-element string, which can consume gigabytes of memory and freeze the browser. Objects are also appended to state rather than paginated or streamed.
findings.reason: A million large objects allocated and put into state.

findings.title: eval executes arbitrary code
findings.explanation: executeUserScript runs its input with eval. Any string, including data originating from user names or input fields, executes with full access to the page and its storage.
findings.reason: eval of arbitrary input.

findings.title: User name injected into executable script
findings.explanation: The 'Say hello' button builds a JavaScript string from user.name and passes it to eval. A name containing a quote and code breaks out and runs arbitrary JavaScript.
findings.reason: user.name interpolated into script passed to eval allows injection. Separate injection site at line 159 not covered by a label.

findings.title: Search input evaluated as code on Enter
findings.explanation: Pressing Enter passes the input value to executeUserScript, which calls eval. Any user, or anyone who tricks a user into pasting text, can execute code. onKeyPress is also deprecated.
findings.reason: Search input passed to eval on Enter.

findings.title: Untyped merge with any and implicit index access
findings.explanation: mergeUserSettings takes any and writes into an untyped {} object by string key, which TypeScript rejects under strict mode. Its behavior is a shallow copy that adds no default values despite the name.
findings.reason: Copying all keys from untrusted input in mergeUserSettings. It flags typing and shallow copy rather than prototype pollution, but it targets the same function and loop.

findings.title: Missing key prop in list rendering
findings.explanation: The users.map callback returns a div without a key. React cannot track items reliably, which can cause incorrect updates and state mix-ups when the list changes.
findings.reason: Missing key prop in list.

findings.title: Sensitive data rendered in the UI
findings.explanation: The dashboard displays user passwords and credit card numbers in plaintext. This exposes sensitive data to anyone viewing the screen, shoulder surfers, and screenshots, and violates basic data-handling practices.
findings.reason: Passwords and card numbers rendered on screen.

findings.title: Unvalidated form data cast to any
findings.explanation: Form values are cast with 'as any' and appended to state without validation or an id. Missing ids break keys and updates, and the password and card number are added to the client model.
findings.reason: Form data cast to any and added to state without an id, which breaks keys and updates, and the password and card number are stored in client state.

findings.title: Search input lacks accessible label
findings.explanation: The search input relies only on a placeholder, which screen readers may not announce reliably, and the form fields are similarly unlabeled.
findings.reason: Accessibility label remark is minor and not a core defect.

findings.title: Monolithic component mixes concerns and lacks error boundary
findings.explanation: One component handles fetching, persistence, search, bulk data generation, scripting, and rendering. There is no error boundary, so any render error crashes the whole dashboard, and the logic is not reusable.
findings.reason: Generic design and architecture remark, speculative.

findings.title: SQL injection through @SortColumn in dynamic SQL
findings.explanation: @SortColumn is a caller-supplied SYSNAME that is concatenated directly into the dynamic SQL text in the ORDER BY clause. It is never validated against a whitelist or passed through QUOTENAME. A caller can pass a value such as 'Name; DROP TABLE dbo.Products; --' or a subquery to run arbitrary statements under the procedure's permissions. Parameterizing the search value on line 17 does not protect this part of the statement.
findings.reason: Identical defect: @SortColumn concatenated into ORDER BY without allow-list or QUOTENAME, enabling SQL injection.

findings.title: Leading wildcard LIKE forces a full scan
findings.explanation: The pattern N'%' + @Search + N'%' begins with a wildcard, so any index on Name cannot be used for a seek. Every row in dbo.Products must be read and evaluated, which gets expensive as the table grows.
findings.reason: Leading-wildcard LIKE does prevent index seeks, but this is inherent to contains-search semantics and is a minor concern; still a plausible performance note. Not a clear defect to fix, so treat as speculative.

findings.title: LIKE wildcards in user input are not escaped
findings.explanation: @Search is inserted into the LIKE pattern without escaping. Characters such as % and _ entered by the user act as wildcards, so a search for '100%' or 'a_b' returns unintended rows.
findings.reason: Unescaped % and _ in user input alter LIKE semantics, so searches for literal '100%' return wrong rows. This is a genuine correctness bug.

findings.title: NULL search value silently returns no rows
findings.explanation: If @Search is passed as NULL, the concatenation yields a NULL @pattern. Name LIKE NULL is never true, so the procedure returns an empty result with no indication to the caller. The procedure does not define whether NULL means 'no filter' or is invalid input.
findings.reason: NULL search returning no rows is standard SQL behavior and a speculative design remark, not a defect.

findings.title: No error handling around dynamic SQL execution
findings.explanation: The procedure has no TRY...CATCH block and no logging. Any failure during dynamic SQL construction or execution, such as an invalid column name in @SortColumn, propagates as a raw error to the caller with no context.
findings.reason: Lack of TRY...CATCH is a best-practice preference; propagating the raw error to the caller is acceptable and often preferable here.

findings.title: Race condition: balance is read and then written without locking, allowing overdrafts and lost updates
findings.explanation: The source balance is read into @Balance at line 14-15 with no locking hint (for example UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK or ROWLOCK), and the debit at line 24 writes back a computed value (@Balance - @Amount) rather than a relative update. Under concurrency, two transfers from the same account can both read the same balance, both pass the check at line 17, and both write, so the account can go negative or one debit is lost. The check and the update are not atomic.
findings.reason: Describes the unlocked read followed by a write-back of a computed value, which allows overdrafts and lost debits under concurrency.

findings.title: NULL @Amount bypasses validation and can null out balances
findings.explanation: The check IF @Amount <= 0 evaluates to UNKNOWN when @Amount is NULL, so the THROW is skipped. Execution continues, the balance check at line 17 also evaluates to UNKNOWN for NULL comparisons, and the UPDATE at line 24 sets Balance = @Balance - NULL, which is NULL. This can wipe out the source account balance and insert a NULL-amount transfer record.
findings.reason: A NULL @Amount makes @Balance < @Amount UNKNOWN, but the IS NULL check does not catch it. The code then goes on to the UPDATE, which would set Balance to NULL. If the Balance column or the Transfers.Amount column is NOT NULL, the statements fail instead. The scenario is plausible, and the reasoning about the UNKNOWN comparisons is valid, so this is a genuine gap. Rechecking: IF @Amount <= 0 with NULL skips the THROW, and the line 17 condition is UNKNOWN, so the block is skipped and the UPDATE runs with a NULL result. That is a real defect not covered by the labels.

findings.title: No TRY/CATCH or XACT_ABORT handling around the transaction
findings.explanation: The procedure opens a transaction at line 12 with no TRY...CATCH block and no SET XACT_ABORT ON. If a runtime error occurs during the UPDATEs or the INSERT (for example a constraint violation, deadlock or timeout), the transaction may be left open or partially applied depending on the error and the caller. Rollback happens only on the explicit validation paths.
findings.reason: Points to the missing XACT_ABORT or TRY/CATCH, which leaves the transaction open after a runtime error.

findings.title: Unknown source account and insufficient funds are conflated in one error
findings.explanation: The same error (50011) is raised when the source account does not exist (NULL balance) and when funds are insufficient. Callers cannot distinguish between a bad account ID and a balance problem, which makes troubleshooting and client handling harder.
findings.reason: Using one error for a missing account and for insufficient funds is a design choice and deliberate here, since the message names both. It is not a defect.

findings.title: Destination existence is checked after the source has already been debited
findings.explanation: The source account is debited at line 23-25 before the destination is verified via @@ROWCOUNT at line 31. This works only because of the rollback, but it does unnecessary write work and relies on the rollback path for correctness.
findings.reason: The rollback does handle the unknown destination correctly, so this is a style or efficiency remark rather than a defect.

findings.title: NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery yields a NULL CustomerId
findings.explanation: If any Orders row matching the year has a NULL CustomerId, the NOT IN predicate evaluates to UNKNOWN for every customer, so the procedure silently returns an empty result set. The results are wrong whenever such a row exists, and the failure is hard to notice.
findings.reason: Describes the NOT IN with NULL CustomerId returning no rows, same as label 1.

findings.title: Non-sargable YEAR() filter on OrderDate
findings.explanation: Wrapping the OrderDate column in YEAR() prevents the optimizer from performing an index seek on OrderDate, forcing a scan of the Orders table for every evaluation.
findings.reason: Identifies the non-sargable YEAR() on OrderDate preventing an index seek, same as label 2.

findings.title: Possible missing supporting index on Orders
findings.explanation: The subquery filters Orders by OrderDate and reads CustomerId. Without an index leading on OrderDate (ideally including CustomerId), the lookup has to scan the full Orders table. The index definitions are not in this file, so this cannot be confirmed.
findings.reason: Speculative missing-index advice that the finding admits cannot be confirmed. Index definitions are not in the file, and the underlying problem is the non-sargable predicate, so this is not a distinct defect.

findings.title: @@IDENTITY used instead of SCOPE_IDENTITY
findings.explanation: @@IDENTITY returns the last identity value generated in the session from any scope, including triggers fired by the INSERT on line 25. If a trigger on dbo.ImportLog inserts into another identity table, @LogId will point to the wrong row, and the staging rows will be tagged with an incorrect ImportLogId.
findings.reason: Identifies @@IDENTITY returning trigger-scope identity instead of SCOPE_IDENTITY, same as label.

findings.title: Cursor used for a row-by-row set operation
findings.explanation: The price update is performed one row at a time through a cursor. For large batches this is slow, generates many round trips and statements, and holds locks for longer. The whole operation can be expressed as a single set-based UPDATE ... FROM join between staging.PriceChanges and dbo.Products.
findings.reason: Cursor row-by-row update should be a set-based UPDATE with join; same defect.

findings.title: Transaction spans the entire row-by-row loop
findings.explanation: The explicit transaction begins before the cursor and remains open while every product row is updated and the log is written. Locks on dbo.Products are held for the full duration, increasing blocking for other sessions on large batches.
findings.reason: Locks held across the row-by-row loop is part of the cursor performance label's rationale; primarily the same loop problem.

findings.title: No TRY/CATCH error handling
findings.explanation: The procedure relies only on SET XACT_ABORT ON. If an error occurs, the transaction is rolled back, but the procedure does not capture the error, log it, or clean up the open cursor. The caller receives a raw error with no context about the batch being processed.
findings.reason: XACT_ABORT ON already rolls back and cursor is deallocated on batch termination; lack of TRY/CATCH is a preference, not a defect.

findings.title: No validation of NewPrice before update
findings.explanation: NewPrice is copied directly into dbo.Products.Price without checking for NULL or negative values. A NULL in staging may violate a constraint and fail the batch, or if the column is nullable it will silently erase a product price.
findings.reason: Speculative; validation of staged data is not shown to be needed, and a NULL would fail a constraint or be a data concern outside this code.

findings.title: Filter column BatchId may lack an index
findings.explanation: The query filters staging.PriceChanges on BatchId and the later update uses the same predicate. Without an index on BatchId, each call scans the staging table, which grows over time.
findings.reason: Speculative index advice with no evidence about the schema; not a defect in this code.

findings.title: OUTPUT parameter retains caller value when no customer is found
findings.explanation: If the caller passes a non-NULL @CustomerId, the SELECT at lines 15-17 assigns nothing when no row matches, because a SELECT with no rows leaves variables unchanged. The IF test at line 19 then sees the caller's stale ID, skips the INSERT, and runs the UPDATE at line 28-30 against that unrelated customer. The procedure can overwrite the wrong customer's name and never creates the new one.
findings.reason: Valid bug: @CustomerId is an OUTPUT param, and a SELECT matching no rows leaves the caller's value unchanged. A non-NULL input would skip the INSERT and update the wrong customer. Fix by setting @CustomerId = NULL before the SELECT.

findings.title: Email is validated after trimming but stored untrimmed
findings.explanation: The validation at line 10 uses LTRIM(RTRIM(@Email)) to reject whitespace-only input, but the lookup at line 17 and the INSERT at line 22 use the raw @Email. Values with leading or trailing spaces are stored as distinct keys, so the same customer can be created more than once depending on how the caller formats the address.
findings.reason: Trimming is only used for the empty check. Storing the raw email is a normalization preference, and SQL Server's default collation already ignores trailing spaces in comparisons. The duplicate-customer claim is speculative.

findings.title: NULL @Name silently overwrites existing names
findings.explanation: @Name is nullable and is not validated. A call with NULL @Name inserts a customer with no name on the INSERT path, and on the UPDATE path at line 29 it overwrites an existing name with NULL. The validation at line 10 only covers @Email.
findings.reason: Whether a NULL name is allowed is a business-rule choice, and the code does not show it to be a defect. The claim is speculative.

findings.title: No TRY...CATCH error handling around the transaction
findings.explanation: The transaction at lines 13-33 has no TRY...CATCH block. XACT_ABORT ON rolls back on error, but the caller gets a raw error with no logging, no context, and no controlled rollback. If the procedure is called inside an outer transaction, an uncommitted or doomed transaction can be left behind without explicit handling.
findings.reason: With XACT_ABORT ON, an error rolls back the transaction automatically and propagates the error. TRY/CATCH here is a best-practice suggestion, not a defect.

findings.title: Rows with NULL Status are silently excluded
findings.explanation: The predicate o.Status <> N'Cancelled' evaluates to UNKNOWN when Status is NULL, so orders with a missing status are dropped from the revenue totals without any signal. If NULL is a valid state for non-cancelled orders, revenue is understated.
findings.reason: The three-valued-logic point is technically accurate, but it is speculative. Nothing indicates Status is nullable or that NULL means non-cancelled, so there is no demonstrated defect.

findings.title: Grouping by a computed expression repeated in SELECT and GROUP BY
findings.explanation: The month-start expression is computed twice (SELECT and GROUP BY) and the GROUP BY on a function of OrderDate cannot use an index on OrderDate for grouping. The date range filter does allow an index seek, but the aggregation still processes every matching row through the expression.
findings.reason: The expression appears in both SELECT and GROUP BY because T-SQL requires that. The date range filter is sargable, and the grouping cost is minor and speculative.

findings.title: Revenue can be NULL for a month with no valid totals
findings.explanation: SUM(o.Total) returns NULL when all Total values in a group are NULL or when the group contains no non-null values, and the result set will return NULL for Revenue without a default. Consumers may not expect NULL in a revenue column.
findings.reason: Months with no rows don't appear at all. A NULL SUM only occurs if every Total in a group is NULL, which is speculative. The finding is a preference for a default.

findings.title: Hardcoded year bounds and error number
findings.explanation: The valid range 2000 to 2100 and the custom error number 50030 are embedded directly in the procedure. Changing the range requires a code change and the error number is not documented.
findings.reason: Hardcoded validation bounds and a custom error number are normal for a stored procedure. This is a style remark, not a defect.

findings.title: No error handling or transaction context
findings.explanation: The procedure has no TRY/CATCH wrapper or logging. While this read-only query is low risk, unexpected failures (for example, a deadlock or a conversion error in Total) will surface raw to callers without context.
findings.reason: A read-only SELECT procedure doesn't need TRY/CATCH or a transaction. This is generic best-practice advice that doesn't matter here.

findings.title: Unencoded query parameter in URL
findings.explanation: The user-provided term is interpolated directly into the URL without encodeURIComponent. Characters such as '&', '#', '=' or '+' alter the request, allowing parameter injection (e.g. adding or overriding API parameters) and producing incorrect searches.
findings.reason: Same defect: the term is interpolated into the URL without encodeURIComponent.

findings.title: Effect has no cleanup; timer and request are never cancelled
findings.explanation: The effect creates an AbortController and a timer but returns no cleanup function. When query or delayMs changes or the component unmounts, the pending timer still fires and the in-flight request is never aborted. The aborted check in the catch block is therefore never triggered by the effect itself. Out-of-order responses from earlier queries can overwrite results for the current query, and state updates can run after unmount.
findings.reason: Same defect: the effect has no cleanup, so the timer is never cleared and the request never aborted, which allows stale responses to overwrite newer results.

findings.title: Unvalidated type assertion on API response
findings.explanation: response.json() returns Promise<any>, and the cast to Product[] is not validated. If the API returns an unexpected shape, the hook silently stores invalid data, which may cause runtime errors downstream when fields like price or name are accessed.
findings.reason: Casting the JSON response to a type is a common pattern. Demanding runtime validation here is a best-practice suggestion, not a defect in this code.

findings.title: Error state not cleared when query is too short
findings.explanation: When the trimmed term is shorter than 2 characters, results are cleared but a previously set error remains. The UI can show a stale error message alongside empty results.
findings.reason: Valid bug: when the term is shorter than 2 characters, results are cleared but the earlier error stays, so the UI can show a stale error next to empty results.

findings.title: Missing explicit return type on exported hook
findings.explanation: The exported hook has no return type annotation, so its public contract is only inferred. Consumers and documentation rely on implicit types.
findings.reason: A missing explicit return type is a style preference. TypeScript infers the type correctly.

findings.title: Mutable Product interface
findings.explanation: Product fields are mutable, which allows consumers to change fetched data accidentally in shared state. Other code paths also do not indicate immutability.
findings.reason: Making interface fields readonly is a speculative preference and does not matter in this code.

findings.title: taxCents returns fractional cents
findings.explanation: taxCents returns (amountCents * ratePercent) / 100 without rounding, so it can return non-integer cent values such as 12.5. The other money helpers (applyCoupon uses Math.round) produce integer cents, so callers can receive inconsistent money values and accumulate rounding drift.
findings.reason: Same defect: taxCents returns unrounded fractional cents.

findings.title: parseQuantity accepts NaN and non-integer quantities
findings.explanation: Number(input) yields NaN for non-numeric strings like 'abc'. NaN < 1 and NaN > 99 are both false, so NaN is returned silently. Inputs like '2.5' also pass the range check and return a fractional quantity, which breaks quantity * unitPriceCents arithmetic.
findings.reason: Same defect: NaN and fractional quantities pass the range check in parseQuantity.

findings.title: formatCents hardcodes a two-decimal currency assumption
findings.explanation: The function always divides by 100, but Intl.NumberFormat already applies each currency's minor-unit digits. For zero-decimal currencies such as JPY, the displayed amount is off by a factor of 100. The function also accepts non-integer cents without validation.
findings.reason: Real defect: dividing by 100 is wrong for zero-decimal currencies like JPY, since the function accepts a currency parameter. Not covered by the labels.

findings.title: Coupon values are not validated
findings.explanation: applyCoupon trusts coupon.percentOff without range checks. A negative percentOff increases the total, a value above 100 is silently clamped to 0, and NaN propagates through Math.round. The Coupon type cannot express these constraints.
findings.reason: Speculative validation advice for coupon data that is presumably trusted; not a concrete defect in this code.

findings.title: Data interfaces are mutable and loosely typed
findings.explanation: CartItem and Coupon have mutable fields and plain number types for money and quantity. Nothing in the type system distinguishes cents from other numbers or prevents accidental mutation of shared cart data.
findings.reason: Style and design preference about branded types and readonly; not a real defect.

findings.title: subtotalCents does not validate inputs
findings.explanation: The reduce trusts unitPriceCents and quantity. Negative, fractional, or NaN values flow into the total without any error, and the function has no error handling for malformed items.
findings.reason: Speculative 'consider validating' advice on internal data; not a concrete defect.

findings.title: Password logged to the console
findings.explanation: console.debug logs the user's plaintext password. Debug output can reach browser devtools, error reporting tools, and shared machines, which exposes credentials.
findings.reason: Same defect: the plaintext password is logged via console.debug on line 19.

findings.title: Unvalidated returnUrl causes an open redirect
findings.explanation: The returnUrl query parameter is passed straight to window.location.assign. An attacker can craft a sign-in link with returnUrl set to an external site, and the user is redirected there after a successful login. The safeReturnUrl helper exists in this file but is never used here.
findings.reason: Same defect: returnUrl goes unvalidated to window.location.assign, and safeReturnUrl is not used.

findings.title: Network failures are not handled
findings.explanation: The fetch call has no try/catch. A network error or aborted request rejects with a generic TypeError, and the caller gets no clear sign-in error message. The non-401 error path is handled, but transport errors are not.
findings.reason: A fetch rejection already propagates to the caller as a rejected promise. Wrapping it in a try/catch only to rewrite the message is a preference, not a defect.

findings.title: useEffect dependency array is missing userId
findings.explanation: The effect reads userId to build the fetch URL but the dependency array is empty. If userId changes while the component stays mounted, the component keeps showing the previous user's profile and never refetches. The cleanup only cancels the stale request when the component unmounts.
findings.reason: Same defect: the effect uses userId but its dependency array is empty, so a userId change never triggers a refetch.

findings.title: Tags are mutated in place and state is set to the same reference
findings.explanation: profile.tags.push(tag) mutates the existing state object, then setProfile(profile) passes the same reference. React uses Object.is to detect changes, so it bails out and does not re-render. The new tag may not appear, and the mutation breaks the immutability React relies on.
findings.reason: Same defect: tags are pushed in place and the same object is passed to setProfile, so React bails out of the re-render.

findings.title: Fetch errors are not handled and the component stays in loading state
findings.explanation: There is no catch for network errors, non-2xx responses, or JSON parse failures. The promise rejects unhandled, and profile stays null, so the user sees 'Loading…' forever with no error message or retry option.
findings.reason: The fetch chain has no catch and does not check r.ok. Failures leave the UI on 'Loading…' forever and produce an unhandled rejection. This is a genuine defect that no label covers.

findings.title: API response is cast to Profile without runtime validation
findings.explanation: r.json() as Promise<Profile> only asserts the type at compile time. If the API returns a different shape, for example a missing tags array, profile.tags.includes or .map will throw at render time.
findings.reason: A type cast on a JSON response is the common pattern here. Asking for runtime validation is speculative best-practice advice and not a defect in this code.

findings.title: Added tags are never persisted to the server
findings.explanation: addTag only updates local component state. There is no request to save the change, so a page reload loses the new tag. The UI suggests the tag was saved when it was not.
findings.reason: The component is not specified to persist tags. This is speculation about missing features rather than a bug in the code.

findings.title: Tag input is not wrapped in a form
findings.explanation: The input and button are not in a form element, so pressing Enter in the input does nothing. Keyboard users have to tab to the button to add a tag.
findings.reason: Wrapping the input in a form for Enter-key submission is a UX preference, not a defect.

findings.title: SQL injection via string concatenation
findings.explanation: The raw req.params.id is concatenated into the SQL text. The parseInt check on line 9 only validates the parsed value, not the string used in the query. An input such as "1 OR 1=1" parses to 1 and passes validation, but the injected SQL is executed.
findings.reason: Same SQL injection via concatenated req.params.id that bypasses the parseInt check.

findings.title: req.user accessed without authentication check or type declaration
findings.explanation: req.user is not part of Express's Request type unless an auth library augments it. If authentication middleware is absent or skipped, req.user is undefined and req.user.id throws a TypeError, resulting in a 500. There is also no check that the caller is authenticated before cancelling an order.
findings.reason: req.user is dereferenced with no auth check and no type augmentation, so it can throw a TypeError. This is a genuine defect that no label covers.

findings.title: Error handler leaks internal error details and stack traces to clients
findings.explanation: The response includes String(err) and err.stack for every error. This exposes internal paths, library versions, and possibly SQL or connection details to any client. The response should not depend on the environment being non-production.
findings.reason: Error handler sends String(err) and stack traces to clients.

findings.title: parseInt accepts partially numeric input
findings.explanation: Number.parseInt('12abc', 10) returns 12, so malformed identifiers like '12abc' or '12.5' are accepted as valid. Combined with the concatenated query, the validated value and the value sent to the database can differ.
findings.reason: parseInt accepts '12abc', so the validated value can differ from the string used in the query. This is a real validation weakness, closely tied to the injection but a distinct defect from it.

findings.title: Non-numeric id in cancel route is not validated
findings.explanation: The /orders/:id/cancel route passes req.params.id directly to Postgres without validation. A non-integer value causes a database type error that falls through to the generic error handler as a 500 instead of a 400.
findings.reason: The cancel route does no id validation, so a non-numeric id causes a DB type error and a 500 instead of a 400. This is a legitimate defect.

findings.title: Ambiguous 409 response for cancel
findings.explanation: A 409 is returned whenever rowCount is not 1. This covers a missing order, an order owned by another customer, and an order not in pending status. Those cases are indistinguishable to the client, and rowCount may be null in pg types, so the check is not safe.
findings.reason: A single 409 for any non-matching update is a reasonable design choice and not a defect. The rowCount null concern is minor.

findings.title: Pool has no error listener and no validation of DATABASE_URL
findings.explanation: An idle client error emitted by pg.Pool without an 'error' listener is an unhandled event that can crash the process. process.env.DATABASE_URL may also be undefined, which is passed silently to the Pool.
findings.reason: pg Pool without an 'error' listener can crash the process on an idle client error. This is a real robustness issue, though the DATABASE_URL part is weaker.

findings.title: Untyped query results and response shapes
findings.explanation: pool.query returns rows typed as any. The response is sent without a declared shape, so there is no compile-time guarantee that the returned object matches what clients expect.
findings.reason: Untyped rows and response shape is a style and typing preference, not a defect.

findings.title: Missing explicit return types on handlers and error handler
findings.explanation: The async route handlers and errorHandler have no explicit return type annotations. Their inferred types mix Response and void across branches, which makes the contract unclear.
findings.reason: Missing explicit return types is a style preference.

findings.title: toDate ignores the 1-based month convention
findings.explanation: CalendarDay documents months as 1-12, but JavaScript's Date constructor expects 0-11. Passing month directly makes every date land one month late, e.g. January (1) becomes February. fromDate adds 1 when reading the month, so the two functions are inconsistent with each other.
findings.reason: Identifies toDate passing 1-based month directly to Date, shifting every date one month late.

findings.title: fromDate returns the weekday instead of the day of the month
findings.explanation: date.getDay() returns the day of the week (0-6), not the day of the month. The day field will be wrong for almost every date. The correct accessor is getDate().
findings.reason: Identifies fromDate using getDay() instead of getDate().

findings.title: addDays inherits the month offset and the wrong day field
findings.explanation: addDays builds its Date through the buggy toDate, which shifts the month forward by one, and then reads the result through the buggy fromDate, which returns the weekday as day. The result is wrong on both counts, so adding days to a date does not produce the intended calendar day.
findings.reason: Describes ts-06-calendar-days#1 but at lines 18-19, outside the window. Describes addDays as a downstream effect of the toDate month offset (and fromDate bug); the primary cause named first is the toDate month shift.

findings.title: isWeekend computes the weekday from a shifted date
findings.explanation: isWeekend calls toDate, which places the date in the wrong month because of the month-indexing bug. The weekday returned by getDay() therefore belongs to a different date, and weekend detection is incorrect.
findings.reason: Describes ts-06-calendar-days#1 but at lines 27-28, outside the window. isWeekend is wrong because toDate shifts the month; the label explicitly mentions isWeekend.

findings.title: No validation of CalendarDay inputs
findings.explanation: toDate and the other functions accept any number. Out-of-range months or days are silently normalized by Date (for example month 13 rolls into the next year), and years 0-99 are mapped to 1900-1999 by the Date constructor. Invalid calendar data therefore produces plausible but wrong dates with no error.
findings.reason: Speculative input validation advice; not a defect in this small utility.

findings.title: CalendarDay fields are mutable
findings.explanation: The interface is used as a value object, but its properties are not readonly. Callers can mutate a day after it has been validated or shared, which can produce inconsistent state.
findings.reason: Readonly fields are a style preference and do not affect correctness here.

findings.title: Errors thrown by the callback are unhandled
findings.explanation: The interval wrapper calls saved.current() without any try/catch. If the callback throws, the exception escapes the timer callback on every tick, and the hook gives callers no way to observe or recover from it.
findings.reason: Letting a callback's exception propagate is standard behavior; swallowing it in a generic hook would be wrong, and there is no defect here.

findings.title: delayMs is not validated for NaN, negative, or non-finite values
findings.explanation: The type number | null accepts NaN, negative numbers, and Infinity. setInterval coerces these to 0 or to a very short delay, which can cause a tight loop that floods the event queue. The type does not express these constraints.
findings.reason: Input validation for NaN, negative or Infinity delays is speculative; this matches the behavior of setInterval and the well-known useInterval pattern, so it is not a defect.

findings.title: Callback ref is updated in useEffect, which runs after paint
findings.explanation: saved.current is set in a passive effect, so during the window between render and effect flush an interval tick can still invoke the previous callback. This is a small staleness window and can cause subtle bugs with closures that depend on the latest props or state.
findings.reason: Updating the ref in an effect is the canonical Dan Abramov pattern. The staleness window is negligible and the code follows accepted practice.

findings.title: Bare return in effect alongside a cleanup-returning path
findings.explanation: The effect returns a bare return on one path and a cleanup function on the other. Under noImplicitReturns, TypeScript can flag this inconsistent return pattern, and it is less explicit than returning undefined.
findings.reason: A bare return in an effect is valid. noImplicitReturns allows a bare return in void-compatible functions, so this is only a style remark.

findings.title: Hardcoded two-decimal assumption breaks zero- and three-decimal currencies
findings.explanation: formatCents always divides by 100 and parseCents always accepts at most two decimal places, regardless of currency. For zero-decimal currencies such as JPY, 1050 cents is formatted from 10.5 and rounds to a wrong whole amount. For three-decimal currencies such as KWD, the value is also wrong.
findings.reason: Dividing by 100 regardless of currency is a genuine limitation: JPY (0 decimals) and KWD (3 decimals) would be formatted incorrectly. The file's contract is explicitly in cents, but the currency parameter makes the mismatch a real defect.

findings.title: Invalid locale or currency throws unhandled runtime errors
findings.explanation: Intl.NumberFormat throws a RangeError for a malformed locale and a TypeError for an invalid currency code. formatCents does not validate or document these cases, so callers receive unexpected exceptions.
findings.reason: Intl.NumberFormat throwing on a malformed locale or invalid currency is standard, expected behavior. The caller is responsible for passing valid values, so this is not a defect in the code.

findings.title: No upper bound on parts allows unbounded array allocation
findings.explanation: splitCents only requires parts to be a positive integer. A large value such as 1e9 makes Array.from allocate a huge array and can exhaust memory or block the event loop.
findings.reason: Allocating an array of size `parts` is inherent to a function that returns `parts` items. The caller controls that size, so this is speculative and not a real bug.

findings.title: Cents represented as plain number with no type distinction
findings.explanation: Cents values and arbitrary numbers share the type number, so callers can pass a major-unit amount to formatCents or splitCents without a compile-time error. This is an easy mistake given the naming alone.
findings.reason: Suggesting branded types is a design preference, not a defect in this code.

findings.title: Runtime input is not validated despite the string type
findings.explanation: parseCents calls input.trim() directly. If untyped JavaScript or a bad JSON payload passes a non-string value, the function throws a TypeError rather than returning null as its contract promises.
findings.reason: The function is typed as taking a string, and defending against untyped callers is speculative best-practice advice rather than a real defect.

findings.title: crypto.randomUUID may be unavailable in some environments
findings.explanation: crypto.randomUUID() is only exposed in secure contexts (HTTPS or localhost) and in newer runtimes. On a plain-HTTP page or an older browser or test environment, calling it throws a TypeError inside the submit handler, so adding a to-do fails with no feedback.
findings.reason: Speculative environment-compatibility concern. crypto.randomUUID is widely supported in modern browsers and secure contexts, and the file has no defect; the label set is empty. Not a genuine bug a senior reviewer would insist on fixing.
